title: Designing Rules to Pick a Rule: Aggregation by Consistency
one_liner: Choose a rank-aggregation rule by asking which rule would reproduce the most stable aggregate ranking if the same data collection were repeated.
lead: Rank aggregation rules often disagree. One rule may favor the top of the list, another may smooth more broadly, and both can look reasonable. This paper asks how to choose among those rules without assuming one fixed data model. Its answer is to choose the rule that would give the most repeatable ranking if you collected similar data again.

problem.h2: Why picking an aggregation rule is hard
paras: When many judges, systems, or users produce rankings, you often need one combined ranking. Social choice and statistics offer many ways to do that, yet different rules can produce different final orders from the same input.

The hard part is one level higher: how do you choose the rule itself? A hand-picked rule may work on one dataset and fail on another because different datasets contain different amounts of noise, disagreement, and tie structure.

callout.html: Pick the aggregation rule whose output stays most consistent across repeated data collection, because a stable rule is less driven by accidental quirks of one sample.

steps.text: Start with several plausible ways to combine rankings.
Create many sampled versions of the dataset so the method can mimic repeated collection.

steps.b: Run each rule on each sample
steps.text: Produce an aggregate ranking for every candidate rule on every sampled dataset.
Score a rule by how similar its aggregate rankings stay across samples, because a stable rule depends less on quirks of one observed dataset.

steps.b: Pick the rule with the highest consistency score
steps.text: Use that rule on the full dataset to produce the final ranking.

paras: The paper changes the criterion for rule selection. Instead of choosing a rule for elegance, habit, or a fixed assumed model, it chooses the rule that gives the most repeatable aggregate ranking under repeated sampling.

hidden.name: aggregation consistency
paras: The hidden quantity is how stable a rule's output ranking would be if the ranking data were collected again. A rule with high consistency changes little from one repeated sample to another, because it captures a strong common ordering signal rather than reacting to random sample noise.
The paper uses this quantity to compare rules directly on the data at hand. That matters because the best rule can differ by dataset, and consistency offers a model-light way to adapt the choice.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark rules whose aggregate rankings stay more stable across repeated samples.

reads.html: A good rule should give nearly the same answer when the data collection is repeated, because stable answers are less likely to be artifacts of one sample.
The rule-picking rule maximizes consistency across sampled replications of the observed ranking data.

paras: A weak aggregation rule is overly sensitive to accidental variation in who ranked what and how. When the sample changes slightly, the final ranking can jump, which means the rule is amplifying noise.
A consistent rule behaves differently. Small changes in the observed rankings leave the aggregate order mostly intact because the rule is capturing the signal that many samples would share.

Sampling provides a practical way to estimate this property. The method cannot rerun the real data collection many times, so it creates many sample versions of the current dataset and asks which rule's outputs agree most across them. That score becomes the rule-selection target.

stages.s: run each candidate rule on each sample

math.words: A rule's score is the average agreement between aggregate rankings produced from many sampled replications of the data.
math.equation: consistency(rule_r) = average over sampled pairs (agreement(aggregate_r(sample_a), aggregate_r(sample_b)))
symbols: two sampled versions of the observed ranking data
the ranking produced by rule_r on one sampled dataset
how similar two aggregate rankings are
the stability score used to pick the rule

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Rule A produces rankings with pairwise agreement scores 0.62, 0.66, and 0.60 across sampled datasets.
Rule B produces agreement scores 0.81, 0.79, and 0.83.
Its average consistency is about 0.81, so Rule B is selected.

math.note: The paper proves exact optimization is hard, so the practical method estimates consistency through sampling.

charts.title: Fixed rule choice
charts.note: This can miss the best rule for a given dataset because the choice is made without looking at repeatability.

charts.title: Consistency-based rule choice
charts.note: This improves rule selection because it favors outputs that survive repeated sampling.

items.b: Sampling may not reflect true recollection.
items.html: If the observed dataset is very small or unrepresentative, sampled copies of it may not mimic real repeated data collection well.

items.b: Most candidate rules may be weak.
items.html: The best rule in a poor candidate set can still be poor, so consistency only helps among the options you provide because selection cannot invent a strong rule that is absent.

items.b: Stability is not the only goal.
items.html: A very stable rule can still miss another property you care about, such as fairness or sensitivity to the very top ranks.
The method is most useful when repeatability is important because stable aggregate rankings are easier to trust in downstream decisions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a ranking dataset with several candidate aggregation rules. Produce many sampled versions of the dataset, score each rule by average ranking agreement across samples, and then compare the selected rule against a fixed default rule.
The selected rule should yield a more stable final ranking under held-out resampling because consistency is the selection target itself.
demo.closing: The demo should show that choosing the rule by repeatability can change the final winner among aggregation rules and can make the final ranking less sample-sensitive.
